name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,639

clue.text: Greek state set back by strikes

indicators.note: to set something back is to move it backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: 'by the door' means 'at the door'
raps are sharp knocks or blows

explanation.surface: A Greek nation hobbled by a wave of industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' suggests walkouts, which fits Greek headlines, but here it means blows; 'by' is not a link but a synonym for 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparta was an ancient city-state of the Peloponnese, famous for its military discipline.

clue.text: Artist isn't breaking through

indicators.note: something breaking into a word splits it open and sits inside it

blocks.note: per is Latin-derived for 'by way of' or 'through'
ain't is the informal form of isn't

explanation.surface: An artist who has failed to make the big breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking through' reads as a phrase about success, but 'breaking' is the insertion signal and 'through' supplies its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter is a straightforward example of an artist, one who works in oils or watercolours.

clue.text: Bits of ginger hair revealing true colour

blocks.note: first meaning: ginger is sold as knobbly underground stems
second meaning: the regrowth at the base of dyed hair shows its natural shade

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a dyed redhead giving the game away; 'ginger' belongs only to the spice in the first meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooks buy fresh ginger as knobbly rhizomes called roots, and the growth nearest the scalp shows natural colour under dye.

clue.text: Cavity appearing shortly after fizzy cola drink

indicators.note: a fizzy liquid bubbles and churns, so the letters are stirred into a new order
made short means cut down, so the final letter is lopped off
turning up after something places one part straight behind another in sequence

blocks.note: taken as written, to be mixed up
a cavity is a hole

explanation.surface: A dentist's warning: a hole in the tooth soon follows a fizzy cola.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavity' and 'fizzy cola' paint a dental picture, while the real definition sits at the end and is a different kind of drink altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcohol is used as a general noun for intoxicating beverages, as in 'he gave up booze'.

clue.text: Eruption from Earth's mantle

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for Earth
the possessive ending taken as written
a mantle is a loose sleeveless cloak, a cape

explanation.surface: Geology: magma bursting up through the layer beneath the crust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mantle' looks like the geological layer, which suits 'Eruption', but it is the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: An escape of gas or steam is a sudden leak or outburst, close to a small eruption.

clue.text: Reforming leader of Ecuador to carry on in charge

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: first letter of the country's name
to last is to continue or carry on
IC is the usual abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A reformist South American president determined to stay in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reforming' looks like a political adjective for the leader, but it is the definition, read as 'forming again'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic material springs back and takes its original shape once more after being stretched.

clue.text: PM's instruction to contact man in Kabul, fellow having disappeared

indicators.note: something that has disappeared is gone, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: 'call me' is an order to get in touch
Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A prime minister ordering officials to reach an Afghan contact after one man went missing.
explanation.walkthrough: James Callaghan was British Labour Prime Minister from 1976 to 1979; the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Callaghan held the office of Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, so he is a former PM.

clue.text: The old man's voting against that Spanish neighbour

blocks.note: pa is a familiar word for father, one's old man
the contraction expanded to 'is'
casting a no is voting against

explanation.surface: Father objects to the Spanish family living next door.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'old man's' looks possessive, but it stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paisano is the Spanish word for a fellow countryman or compatriot, someone from the same place.

clue.text: Butcher in choir appals new clergyman

indicators.note: to butcher is to hack apart and mangle, so these letters are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A tradesman singing in church upsets the newly arrived vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' reads as a man in the choir, but it is a verb telling you to hack the letters about.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplain attached to a jail is a minister of religion, so he is one kind of clergyman.

clue.text: Creator of law for police that keeps one on the beat?

definitions.text: that keeps one on the beat?

blocks.note: PACE is the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, which governs police powers in England and Wales
a maker is one who creates something

explanation.surface: A legislator who writes police rules that keep the officer walking the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: A maker of PACE is a PACE maker. The beat is the policeman's round in the surface, but the heartbeat in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical implant regulates the heart's rhythm electrically, keeping its rhythm steady; the question mark flags the punning.

clue.text: Read out scene's quotes

indicators.note: reading something out means saying it, so we go by how the word is pronounced

blocks.note: a scene is a site or location, and 'sites' is how the word is pronounced

explanation.surface: Reading aloud the dialogue from a scene of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 'scene's' is a plural in disguise: scenes are sites.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite a source is to quote it as evidence or authority, a straightforward synonym in verb form.

clue.text: Bestseller list affected some local shops

blocks.note: something hit by a change has been affected by it
a parade is a British word for a short row of local shops

explanation.surface: The bestseller charts have hurt the trade of small neighbourhood stores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'list' looks like the end of the subject, but 'Bestseller list' is the whole definition and 'affected' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The hit parade is a dated name for the weekly chart ranking the best-selling pop records.

clue.text: Spring treat, say, including special rates for one

indicators.note: a special arrangement is an unusual one, so the letters go into a different order
to include something is to hold it within, so one part wraps round the rest

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates 'for example', which 'say' also means
taken as written, to be rearranged
e.g. means 'for one example'

explanation.surface: A seasonal chocolate offered at a discount.
explanation.walkthrough: The two abbreviations are the same: one goes round the rearranged letters and the other sits after them inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate eggs are the traditional sweet given at the Christian festival held each year in March or April.

clue.text: Within wedlock, educated woman catches French disease?  On the contrary

indicators.note: to catch is to trap or hold, so one part ends up enclosed by the other
this reverses who holds whom, so the instruction just given is turned around

blocks.note: mal is French for illness or pain
from Willy Russell's play and film 'Educating Rita'

explanation.surface: A scandal: a married academic catches a sexually transmitted disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French disease' is an old euphemism for syphilis, which steers you wrong. 'On the contrary' reverses the containment, so the disease holds the woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Marital describes things belonging to marriage, so it means relating to or inside a married union.

clue.text: Violent dispute at narrow junction's beginning to get sorted

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted
sorting things out puts them into a fresh order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Road rage at a tight crossing that needs settling.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a traffic quarrel; the definition is understated, since the dispute was a ten-year war.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary conflict between Greeks and Trojans over Helen was a famously bloody quarrel, so the phrase is an understatement.

clue.text: Collusion starts to cause angry calls from Parliament

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: opening letters of the two words
MPs hoot and jeer during noisy debates in the House of Commons

explanation.surface: A scandal of secret dealings provokes uproar in the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' looks like 'begins to', but it means the first letters of the next words.
explanation.definitionFit: To be 'in cahoots' is to be in secret partnership, so the word stands for conspiring together.

clue.text: Important part of course giving entry to Yale?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

blocks.note: key means crucial or important
a golf course is made up of eighteen holes

explanation.surface: A crucial module on the syllabus that gets you into a top American university.
explanation.walkthrough: Yale looks like the university, but here it is the Yale lock brand; the course is a golf course, not an academic one.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yale lock is opened through its slot, so the aperture admits the key to the lock mechanism.

clue.text: Two pointers at the table given chicken beginning to slobber

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: both mean cowardly
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Two dogs drooling at the dinner table after being given chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Pointers seem to be gun dogs begging for food, but the table is a snooker table, where the yellow ball scores two points.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker each yellow ball potted scores two points, so yellows are balls worth a pair of points.

clue.text: Saying mass lifts all even from despair

indicators.note: even-numbered positions are the second, fourth and sixth, so only those letters survive
in a down entry, to lift something is to hold it above you, so one part sits on top of another

blocks.note: letters 2, 4 and 6 of the word
a gram is a unit of mass

explanation.surface: The Catholic service raises everyone's spirits out of hopelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' suggests the church service but is a unit of weight; in this down clue it holds the selected letters above it.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short, pithy remark, a witty maxim or proverb.

clue.text: Dress and dressing: part of verb and a gerund

definitions.note: covers both the verb and the noun senses

indicators.note: only a portion of the following words is taken, the run of letters sitting inside them

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of the first word through the start of the last

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: a verb and its gerund.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a neat joke: the word is a verb meaning 'dress' and a noun meaning 'dressing', just as the clue says 'verb and a gerund'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bandage a wound is to dress it, and the strip of gauze itself is a surgical dressing.

clue.text: Pilot with long limbs, good at higher altitude

indicators.note: in a down entry, a higher altitude means further up the column, so that letter is taken out and moved up

blocks.note: big in size, long or tall
G is the abbreviation for good
legs are limbs

explanation.surface: A lanky airman who flies well at height.
explanation.walkthrough: The G already in the word for limbs climbs to the top of it. Biggles is the flying ace of W. E. Johns's children's adventure books.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain James Bigglesworth, nicknamed Biggles, is a fictional fighter pilot hero of boys' stories.

clue.text: Pick an argument on the phone

indicators.note: on the phone you only hear words spoken, so we go by how they sound

blocks.note: a point is an argument made in a debate

explanation.surface: Deliberately starting a row during a call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick an argument' reads as 'pick a fight', but 'Pick' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To appoint someone to a post is to choose or select them, so it means to pick.

clue.text: Action taken after firing director during regional reshuffle

indicators.note: a reshuffle mixes things into a new order, as with a pack of cards
something happening during a process is caught up in it, so this letter joins the mix

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for director
taken as written

explanation.surface: Office politics: a manager is sacked in the middle of a regional restructuring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firing director' reads as a dismissal, but 'firing' belongs to the definition and means shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: After shooting a gun, you put fresh ammunition in it ready to shoot again.

clue.text: Chart the Québécois growth, notably in Canada

blocks.note: a chart is a map
le is French for 'the', as spoken in Quebec

explanation.surface: Mapping the expansion of French-speaking Quebec within Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growth' sounds economic, but it is a tree; the leaf of this tree is on the Canadian flag.
explanation.definitionFit: Maple trees grow widely across Canada and the maple leaf is the national emblem.

clue.text: Deer are imitating cattle all around London

blocks.note: moo is the sound cattle make
the South East of England is the region that surrounds London

explanation.surface: Herds of deer around the capital are mimicking cows.
explanation.walkthrough: The South East is the English administrative region that encircles Greater London on every side.
explanation.definitionFit: The moose is the largest species of the deer family, called an elk in Europe.

clue.text: Cheeky ladies' man with a plan?

blocks.note: a forward person is bold or cheeky
the ladies' is a women's toilet, a loo
a king is a chess piece, or man

explanation.surface: A cheeky womaniser with a scheme to seduce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ladies' man' looks like a single phrase for a womaniser, but it splits into the toilet and the chess piece; loo is British slang for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward-looking person plans for the future, so having a plan is a loose, question-marked sense.

clue.text: Religious community remains jolly about the onset of apocalypse

indicators.note: an onset is a start, so only the opening letter is wanted
to be about something is to go around it, enclosing it

blocks.note: ash is what remains after burning
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sect stays cheerful as the end of the world approaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remains' looks like a verb (stays) but is the noun; 'jolly' looks like an adjective but is a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a Hindu hermitage or retreat where a spiritual group lives together.

clue.text: We stay out, lubricated, naturally

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Partygoers who stay out late, well oiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lubricated' suggests drunk, the usual slang, but the definition means slick with the body's own moisture.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweaty body is moistened by perspiration, which the skin produces naturally, so it is self-lubricated.
